primitives.name: Hold Usage Detection
primitives.verbatim_quote: We show that a frozen, off-the-shelf pose foundation model is sufficient: using the fingertip and toe keypoints of Sapiens, a per-frame proximity test against the annotated holds, per-limb mutual exclusion, and a short temporal-persistence rule, we detect hold usage without any climbing-specific training.

primitives.assumptions: Pose keypoints accurately localize fingertips and toes; holds are statically annotated; occlusion does not prevent keypoint detection.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When limb occlusion exceeds 50% or keypoint localization fails due to lighting.

layer2.mapping: The derived kernel computes temporal intervals of limb-hold contact using proximity scores and mutual exclusion constraints.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that hold usage detection in sport climbing can be achieved without task-specific training by leveraging frozen, off-the-shelf pose models such as Sapiens. The system uses fingertip and toe keypoints to compute proximity to annotated holds, applying a per-frame proximity test. Temporal persistence ensures that transient contacts are filtered out, and mutual exclusion prevents contradictory limb assignments. These primitives form a minimal yet effective framework for detecting hold usage. The failure mode arises from occlusion, which affects both hand and foot keypoint visibility, particularly in dense climbing scenarios. The system's robustness stems from its reliance on precise keypoint localization rather than coarse body part estimates. The temporal rule acts as a smoothing mechanism, filtering noise from brief, spurious interactions. The mutual exclusion constraint aligns with biomechanical realism, ensuring that only one limb interacts with a hold at a time. The pipeline's success hinges on the fidelity of the pose estimator and the quality of the hold annotations. The method outperforms prior work using wrist/ankle keypoints, which suffer from spatial misalignment and occlusion issues. The ablation study confirms that adding dense feature gating or segmentation degrades performance, underscoring the efficacy of a minimal keypoint-only approach.
